newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers line roads in stand-off with police.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers line roads in stand-off with police.

text.p: Protesting farmers lined the sides of Greece's main north-south road with thousands of tractors on Friday after socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis refused to meet them and discuss their economic demands.
Police deflated the tractor tyres to stop farmers from moving their vehicles to the middle of the highways and banned farmers and the press from access to the scene, the farmers said.
"The government has taken all measures to keep highways free," Simitis told parliament on Friday. "The government will never succumb to blackmail."
Simitis refused to bow to a farmers' ultimatum on Thursday to meet them and discuss their demands. The farmers answered with a mass parade of 2,000 tractors on the main north-south highway.

Now facing critisism for taking no action when the farmers occupied highways for 25 days in December, the government sent 5,000 police, many in riot gear, into the central Thessaly region with strict orders to keep roads open.

Flexing their muscles, the farmers eluded police on Thursday night, driving their tractors for five hours through cotton fields and across rivers before emerging on the national highway outside the central Almiros village.
Television showed the convoy of tractors -- an endless line of headlights coming in from the mountains -- rattling down the highway as police units watched from a distance.
After farmers left their a line of tractors about five km (three miles) long by the road near Almyros in central Greece, police cordoned off the area.
Farmers said their tyres had been deflated to immobilize them. Television showed some tractors with deflated tyres.
"What the government did is despicable," farmers' representative Vangelis Boutas told reporters. "They want to block our tractors and then force us to talk."

The farmers have been playing a cat-and-mouse game with police for the past four days, driving their tractors off the roads and across vast farmlands or under bridges whenever riot squads and police helicopters confronted them.
They blocked smaller roads at will in a bid to show that police could not stop them from repeating their December action.
Simitis waited out that 25-day blockade, saying the country could not afford to satisfy the farmers' demands, which include cheaper fuel, lower taxes and more subsidies.
The farmers gave up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands were not met.
They are among a long list of groups protesting or striking against a 1997 budget described as the toughest in 15 years, and strict incomes and tax policies.
Teachers are on strike for a third week while labour confederations have staged repeated walkouts against the government. Protest rallies almost daily congest traffic in the Greek capital.
Simitis has turned down all labour demands, saying giving in would risk Greece's efforts to catch up with its European Union partners.
